questions.question: Define static load, distinguishing dead load from live load, and explain why static loads are the more predictable part of structural design.
questions.expected_answer: A static load is a force that does not change with time. Dead load is the permanent weight of the structure itself, such as the concrete slab, fill, kerb and rails of the ramp. Live load is load from use, such as a parked wheelchair or standing people, which while present is steady. Static loads are predictable because material weights are known, so dead load can be calculated exactly from the drawing, for example about 1.3 cubic metres of concrete at 2 400 kilograms per cubic metre gives about 3 100 kilograms, and the ground can be checked to carry it.

questions.question: Give three examples of dynamic loads on the stairs and ramp and explain two reasons why dynamic loads are more severe than static loads of the same size.
questions.expected_answer: Examples: a crowd running down the stairs at the bell, a learner jumping the last steps, a wheelchair bumping over a join, a crowd leaning on the handrail, wind on a long rail. Reasons: impact, because a moving mass must be stopped and stopping it quickly needs a force several times its weight; and repetition, because loads applied thousands of times over years grow small cracks through fatigue even though no single load approaches the breaking load. Designers respond with thicker reinforced treads and landings, posts set deep and rails designed for sideways push, and protected step nosings.

questions.question: Distinguish between even and uneven loads with examples from the ramp, and explain why a concentrated load can be more dangerous than a larger distributed one.
questions.expected_answer: An even or uniformly distributed load is spread equally over a surface, such as the slab's own weight on fill or a landing full of standing people, so every part of the structure shares it. An uneven load is concentrated or varies, such as a wheelchair's four small wheels, a trolley wheel on the kerb or a crowd bunched at one end of a landing. A concentrated load produces high local pressure and, if the slab is unsupported beneath, such as over a washed-out hollow, bends it as a beam, which is how slabs crack; uneven loads also create turning effects that can tip a landing or lever a post from its base.
